claim: Toxoplasma gondii infects 30-40% of the world's population.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that infects 30–40% of the world's population.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bigna et al., 2020; Flegr et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2009) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: T. gondii infections are typically subclinical in immunocompetent individuals.
source: T. gondii infections are typically subclinical in immunocompetent individuals but may cause blindness (Rothova, 1993; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rothova, 1993; Su et al., 2014).

claim: T. gondii infections can cause blindness in immunocompetent individuals.
source: T. gondii infections are typically subclinical in immunocompetent individuals but may cause blindness (Rothova, 1993; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rothova, 1993; Su et al., 2014).

claim: T. gondii infections can be life-threatening in immunocompromised individuals and the developing fetus.
source: In immunocompromised individuals and the developing fetus, the disease can be life-threatening (Pappas et al., 2009; Elsheikha et al., 2021; McLeod et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pappas et al., 2009; Elsheikha et al., 2021; McLeod et al., 2014).

claim: The pathogenesis of acute T. gondii infection is caused by the highly motile tachyzoite life-cycle stage.
source: T. gondii is a single-cell protozoan, and the pathogenesis associated with acute infection is caused by the highly motile tachyzoite life-cycle stage.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript based on established knowledge about T. gondii biology.

claim: T. gondii tachyzoites use a unique form of substrate-dependent motility to invade and egress from host cells.
source: Like other apicomplexan parasites, the T. gondii tachyzoite uses a unique form of substrate-dependent motility to invade into and egress from cells of its host, to migrate across biological barriers, and to disseminate throughout the infected host.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about apicomplexan parasite biology.

claim: Motility is central to the pathogenesis of toxoplasmosis.
source: Motility is, therefore, central to the pathogenesis of toxoplasmosis (Barragan et al., 2005; Harker et al., 2015; Meissner et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Barragan et al., 2005; Harker et al., 2015; Meissner et al., 2002).

claim: T. gondii parasites have no cilia or flagella.
source: The parasite has no cilia or flagella and can move at speeds of up to 3 µm/s without the leading edge protrusions that drive the substrate-dependent motility of other eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about T. gondii morphology.

claim: T. gondii parasites can move at speeds of up to 3 µm/s.
source: The parasite has no cilia or flagella and can move at speeds of up to 3 µm/s without the leading edge protrusions that drive the substrate-dependent motility of other eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about T. gondii motility.

claim: Within a 3D extracellular matrix, T. gondii parasites move along a complex helical trajectory characterized by regular oscillations in velocity and changes in trajectory curvature and torsion.
source: Within a three-dimensional (3D) extracellular matrix, the parasite moves along a complex helical trajectory characterized by regular oscillations in velocity and changes in trajectory curvature and torsion (Leung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Leung et al., 2014).

claim: Motility is driven by a complex of proteins known as the glideosome, which is anchored to the inner membrane complex at the parasite periphery.
source: Motility is driven, at least in part, by a complex of proteins known as the glideosome, which is anchored to the inner membrane complex at the parasite periphery (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on established knowledge about the glideosome.

claim: In the linear motor model of motility, short actin filaments are bound through TgGAC to the cytosolic tails of transmembrane adhesins such as TgMIC2.
source: In the 'linear motor' model of motility, short actin filaments are bound through the bridging protein TgGAC to the cytosolic tails of transmembrane adhesins, such as TgMIC2, and translocated toward the posterior end of the parasite via a class XIV myosin, TgMyoA (Frénal et al., 2017; Heintzelman, 2015; Jacot et al., 2016; Sibley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Frénal et al., 2017; Heintzelman, 2015; Jacot et al., 2016; Sibley, 2004).

claim: In the linear motor model, actin filaments are translocated toward the posterior end of the parasite via TgMyoA.
source: In the 'linear motor' model of motility, short actin filaments are bound through the bridging protein TgGAC to the cytosolic tails of transmembrane adhesins, such as TgMIC2, and translocated toward the posterior end of the parasite via a class XIV myosin, TgMyoA (Frénal et al., 2017; Heintzelman, 2015; Jacot et al., 2016; Sibley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Frénal et al., 2017; Heintzelman, 2015; Jacot et al., 2016; Sibley, 2004).

claim: If the extracellular domains of transmembrane adhesins are attached to ligands on the substrate, the rearward translocation of actin results in forward movement of the parasite.
source: If the extracellular domains of the transmembrane adhesins are attached to ligands on the substrate, the rearward translocation of actin results in forward movement of the parasite.
evidence: This is a description of the linear motor model mechanism based on established theory.

claim: Other apicomplexan parasites, including Plasmodium spp. and Cryptosporidium spp., express similar glideosome proteins.
source: Other apicomplexan parasites, including those that cause malaria (Plasmodium spp.) and cryptosporidiosis (Cryptosporidium spp.), express similar glideosome proteins, suggesting that the mechanism of motility is conserved (Kappe et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kappe et al., 1999).

claim: The mechanism of motility is conserved among apicomplexan parasites.
source: Other apicomplexan parasites, including those that cause malaria (Plasmodium spp.) and cryptosporidiosis (Cryptosporidium spp.), express similar glideosome proteins, suggesting that the mechanism of motility is conserved (Kappe et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the observation that similar proteins are expressed, with citation support (Kappe et al., 1999).

claim: Abundant evidence supports the importance of TgMyoA and other components of the glideosome in motility.
source: Although abundant evidence supports the importance of TgMyoA and other components of the glideosome in motility (Meissner et al., 2002; Jacot et al., 2016; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Tosetti et al., 2019; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Frénal et al., 2010), several recent observations have raised questions about whether these proteins generate force as described by the linear motor model and, if so, whether this is the only motility mechanism available to the parasite (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Gras et al., 2019; Meissner et al., 2013; Tardieux and Baum, 2016; Whitelaw et al., 2017; Rompikuntal et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Meissner et al., 2002; Jacot et al., 2016; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Tosetti et al., 2019; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Frénal et al., 2010).

claim: Recent observations have raised questions about whether glideosome proteins generate force as described by the linear motor model.
source: Although abundant evidence supports the importance of TgMyoA and other components of the glideosome in motility (Meissner et al., 2002; Jacot et al., 2016; Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Tosetti et al., 2019; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Frénal et al., 2010), several recent observations have raised questions about whether these proteins generate force as described by the linear motor model and, if so, whether this is the only motility mechanism available to the parasite (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Gras et al., 2019; Meissner et al., 2013; Tardieux and Baum, 2016; Whitelaw et al., 2017; Rompikuntal et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Gras et al., 2019; Meissner et al., 2013; Tardieux and Baum, 2016; Whitelaw et al., 2017; Rompikuntal et al., 2021).

claim: The linear motor model predicts continuous anterior-to-posterior forces along the entire periphery of the moving parasite.
source: The linear motor model predicts continuous anterior-to-posterior forces along the entire periphery of the moving parasite.
evidence: This is a description of a prediction from the linear motor model based on established theory.

claim: Fluorescent microspheres embedded within Matrigel are pulled towards a moving parasite from nearby anterior, posterior, and lateral locations within the matrix.
source: Fluorescent microspheres embedded within the Matrigel were pulled towards a moving parasite from nearby anterior, posterior, and lateral locations within the matrix, and these microspheres returned to their original positions after the parasite had passed (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Fluorescent microspheres return to their original positions after the parasite has passed.
source: Fluorescent microspheres embedded within the Matrigel were pulled towards a moving parasite from nearby anterior, posterior, and lateral locations within the matrix, and these microspheres returned to their original positions after the parasite had passed (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The parasite exerts a detectable force on the surrounding matrix.
source: These results demonstrate that the parasite does indeed exert a detectable force on the surrounding matrix.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that microspheres are displaced toward the moving parasite.

claim: Constrictions form in the body of the parasite as it moves.
source: Unexpectedly, we also noted constrictions in the body of the fluorescent parasite as it moved (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 2.

claim: Each constriction forms at the apical end of the parasite and remains stationary relative to the matrix as the parasite moves through.
source: Each constriction formed at the apical end of the parasite and remained stationary relative to the matrix as the parasite moved through, reminiscent of the 'moving junction' through which the parasite penetrates during host cell invasion (discussed further below).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claim: All wild-type parasites analyzed (n=99) formed at least one constriction per body length of motility.
source: All wild-type parasites analyzed (n=99) formed at least one constriction per body length of motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 99 parasites.

claim: Parasite motility in matrices generated using 2.25 mg/ml fibrinogen is indistinguishable from that observed in Matrigel.
source: Parasite motility in matrices generated using 2.25 mg/ml fibrinogen was indistinguishable from that observed in Matrigel (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parasites moving through fluorescent fibrin deform the matrix.
source: Visual comparison of successive image volumes confirmed that parasites moving through fluorescent fibrin also deform the matrix (Figure 2C and Video 5) and undergo constrictions (see below) similar to those observed in Matrigel.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 5.

claim: The limit of detection for 3D displacement magnitudes in the system ranges from 42 to 46 nm.
source: Using this approach, the limit of detection for 3D displacement magnitudes in the system ranges from 42 to 46 nm; a similar 3D displacement detection threshold (43–46 nm) was observed in samples containing no parasites (see Figure 6E below), validating the approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and validation using samples without parasites (Figure 6E).

claim: When analyzing data in the x-y plane only, the displacement detection threshold is 28-31 nm.
source: When analyzing data in the x-y plane only, the background cutoff was calculated using the x-y displacement magnitudes (rather than the x-y-z displacement magnitudes); this lowered the displacement detection threshold to 28–31 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis methods.

claim: The fibrin gel behaves as a predominantly elastic matrix.
source: The fibrin gel behaves as a predominantly elastic matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with an elastic modulus of 15.6 pN/µm and a viscous modulus of 0.09 pN*s/µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from laser trapping measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elastic modulus of the fibrin matrix is 15.6 pN/µm.
source: The fibrin gel behaves as a predominantly elastic matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with an elastic modulus of 15.6 pN/µm and a viscous modulus of 0.09 pN*s/µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from laser trapping measurements.

claim: The viscous modulus of the fibrin matrix is 0.09 pN*s/µm.
source: The fibrin gel behaves as a predominantly elastic matrix (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with an elastic modulus of 15.6 pN/µm and a viscous modulus of 0.09 pN*s/µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from laser trapping measurements.

claim: The minimal detectable force magnitude in the system is 0.66-0.72 pN in 3D.
source: The minimal detectable force magnitude in this system is therefore 0.66–0.72 pN in 3D and 0.45–0.49 pN in the x-y plane.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the displacement detection threshold and the elastic modulus of the matrix.

claim: The minimal detectable force magnitude in the x-y plane is 0.45-0.49 pN.
source: The minimal detectable force magnitude in this system is therefore 0.66–0.72 pN in 3D and 0.45–0.49 pN in the x-y plane.
evidence: This claim is calculated from the displacement detection threshold and the elastic modulus of the matrix.

claim: The matrix deforms in toward the parasite from all x-y directions at discrete, periodic time points along the trajectory.
source: Plotting fibrin displacement as x-y maps showed that the matrix deforms in toward the parasite from all x-y directions at discrete, periodic time points along the trajectory, before relaxing back to its initial position (e.g., Figure 4A–D and Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: The matrix relaxes back to its initial position after deformation.
source: Plotting fibrin displacement as x-y maps showed that the matrix deforms in toward the parasite from all x-y directions at discrete, periodic time points along the trajectory, before relaxing back to its initial position (e.g., Figure 4A–D and Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: The matrix is simultaneously pulled in toward the parasite in all three dimensions.
source: Viewing the data as projections along each axis demonstrates that the matrix is simultaneously pulled in toward the parasite in all three dimensions (Video 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Video 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In approximately 50% of cases, inward deformation occurred between two consecutive image volumes (1.6 seconds apart) and was followed in the next image volume by relaxation.
source: In approximately 50% of cases, inward deformation occurred between two consecutive image volumes (1.6 seconds apart) and was followed in the next image volume by relaxation (e.g., Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: In most other cases, the inward deformation was held through multiple time points before relaxing.
source: In most other cases, the inward deformation was held through multiple time points before relaxing (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: During periods of motility when the matrix was not being pulled inward or relaxing outward, little deformation of the matrix above background was detectable.
source: During periods of motility when the matrix was not being pulled inward or relaxing outward, little deformation of the matrix above background was detectable (e.g. Figure 4C, leftmost and rightmost panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The timing of each large matrix deformation coincides with the presence of a parasite constriction.
source: When the displacement maps were overlaid onto the images of the moving parasites, it was immediately apparent that the timing of each large matrix deformation coincided with the presence of a parasite constriction and that the displacement vectors pointed primarily in towards the constriction (Figure 4C and D; additional examples are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The displacement vectors point primarily in towards the constriction.
source: When the displacement maps were overlaid onto the images of the moving parasites, it was immediately apparent that the timing of each large matrix deformation coincided with the presence of a parasite constriction and that the displacement vectors pointed primarily in towards the constriction (Figure 4C and D; additional examples are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pinching of the parasite membrane results from pulling forces generated by the parasite rather than the parasite squeezing through a narrow pore within the matrix.
source: The fact that the displacements were directed inwards rather than away from the parasite indicates that the pinching of the parasite membrane results from pulling forces generated by the parasite rather than the parasite squeezing through a narrow pore within the matrix, which would push the matrix away.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the direction of the displacement vectors observed in the experimental data.

claim: The time it took a parasite to move completely through a constriction ranged from 1.6 to 56.2 seconds (average 6.8±5.2 seconds).
source: The time it took a parasite to move completely through a constriction ranged from 1.6 to 56.2 seconds (average 6.8±5.2 seconds, measured in brightfield; n=99 parasites, 188 constrictions) with the longer times due to a stall in forward progression of a constricting parasite.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 99 parasites and 188 constrictions.

claim: In 46% of cases, the end of one constriction was followed immediately by the beginning of another.
source: In 46% of the cases, the end of one constriction was followed immediately by the beginning of another, while in 14% of the cases a second constriction would start before the first constriction finished (Figure 5A and B and Video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B and Video 9.

claim: In 14% of cases, a second constriction starts before the first constriction finishes.
source: In 46% of the cases, the end of one constriction was followed immediately by the beginning of another, while in 14% of the cases a second constriction would start before the first constriction finished (Figure 5A and B and Video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B and Video 9.

claim: The speed of the parasite's forward motion increases once the constriction passes the halfway point on the parasite's longitudinal axis.
source: The speed of the parasite's forward motion changed as it moved through the constriction, increasing once the constriction passed the halfway point on the parasite's longitudinal axis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; n=20 parasites, 24 constrictions).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 from analysis of 20 parasites and 24 constrictions.

claim: All parasites that move at least one body length undergo a constriction.
source: Most importantly, all parasites that move at least one body length undergo a constriction and the total trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions observed (Figure 5C), strongly suggesting that the parasite-generated forces that create the constriction play an important role in forward movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The total trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions observed.
source: Most importantly, all parasites that move at least one body length undergo a constriction and the total trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions observed (Figure 5C), strongly suggesting that the parasite-generated forces that create the constriction play an important role in forward movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The parasite-generated forces that create the constriction play an important role in forward movement.
source: Most importantly, all parasites that move at least one body length undergo a constriction and the total trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions observed (Figure 5C), strongly suggesting that the parasite-generated forces that create the constriction play an important role in forward movement.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that all moving parasites undergo constrictions and trajectory length is proportional to constriction number.

claim: The width of a constricting parasite at the midway point is 1.4±0.2 µm compared to 2.6±0.4 µm before constriction.
source: The much reduced width of a constricting parasite (2.6±0.4 µm vs. 1.4±0.2 µm at the midway point along the parasite's longitudinal axis before and during a constriction, respectively; Figure 5D, n=15 parasites, 19 constrictions) led us to question whether the constriction presents a physical obstacle to the forward motion of the nucleus (normal nuclear diameter measured by DNA staining = 2.0 ± 0.3 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D from analysis of 15 parasites and 19 constrictions.

claim: The normal nuclear diameter measured by DNA staining is 2.0 ± 0.3 µm.
source: The much reduced width of a constricting parasite (2.6±0.4 µm vs. 1.4±0.2 µm at the midway point along the parasite's longitudinal axis before and during a constriction, respectively; Figure 5D, n=15 parasites, 19 constrictions) led us to question whether the constriction presents a physical obstacle to the forward motion of the nucleus (normal nuclear diameter measured by DNA staining = 2.0 ± 0.3 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DNA staining measurements.

claim: The parasite nucleus becomes thinner and more elongate as it passes through the constriction.
source: In parasites labeled with both a fluorescent DNA stain and a fluorescently labeled antibody against the major surface protein, TgSAG1 (to visualize the constriction), the normally round parasite nucleus did indeed become thinner and more elongate as it passed through the constriction and regained its round shape once it was through (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The nucleus regains its round shape once it passes through the constriction.
source: In parasites labeled with both a fluorescent DNA stain and a fluorescently labeled antibody against the major surface protein, TgSAG1 (to visualize the constriction), the normally round parasite nucleus did indeed become thinner and more elongate as it passed through the constriction and regained its round shape once it was through (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ratio of nuclear dimensions perpendicular and parallel to the long axis of the parasite is 0.93±0.08 in a non-constricting parasite and 0.50±0.06 as the nucleus passes through a constriction.
source: The ratio of the nuclear dimensions perpendicular and parallel to the long axis of the parasite was 0.93±0.08 in a non-constricting parasite and 0.50±0.06 as the nucleus passed through a constriction (n=9 parasites, 21 constrictions).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 9 parasites and 21 constrictions.

claim: The distribution of fluorescent anti-TgSAG1 antibody on the parasite surface changes as the parasite moves.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of the fluorescent anti-TgSAG1 antibody on the parasite surface changed as the parasite moved: much of the fluorescent signal appeared to be 'swept' from anterior to posterior at the constriction as the parasite moved through (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10.

claim: The redistributed antibody is ultimately shed and deposited behind the moving parasite in the form of a fluorescent helical trail within the Matrigel.
source: The redistributed antibody was ultimately shed and deposited behind the moving parasite in the form of a fluorescent helical trail within the Matrigel (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10.

claim: All moving parasites examined (n=9) deposited trails containing anti-SAG1 in the Matrigel.
source: All moving parasites examined (n=9) deposited trails containing anti-SAG1 in the Matrigel.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 9 parasites.

claim: Only 18 of 769 TgMyoA knockout parasites examined (2%) moved one body length or more during a 302-second time course.
source: As previously reported (Whitelaw et al., 2017), these parasites are much less motile in 3D than wild-type parasites: only 18 of 769 TgMyoA knockout parasites examined (2%) moved one body length or more during a 302-second time course, compared to 99 of 278 wild-type parasites (36%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 769 TgMyoA knockout parasites and citation to prior work (Whitelaw et al., 2017).

claim: 99 of 278 wild-type parasites (36%) moved one body length or more during a 302-second time course.
source: As previously reported (Whitelaw et al., 2017), these parasites are much less motile in 3D than wild-type parasites: only 18 of 769 TgMyoA knockout parasites examined (2%) moved one body length or more during a 302-second time course, compared to 99 of 278 wild-type parasites (36%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 278 wild-type parasites.

claim: None of the TgMyoA knockout parasites that moved at least one body length showed clear constrictions at a fixed point within the matrix like those seen in wild-type parasites.
source: Of the 18 TgMyoA knockout parasites that moved at least one body length (e.g. Figure 6A), none showed clear constrictions at a fixed point within the matrix like those seen in wild-type parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 18 TgMyoA knockout parasites shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TgMyoA knockout parasites move in tightly twisting arcs or in a stair-like pattern consisting of right-angled turns associated with a sharp bend in the body of the parasite.
source: The pattern of movement was also different from wild-type parasites; rather than moving along smooth helical trajectories, the TgMyoA knockout parasites moved in tightly twisting arcs or in a stair-like pattern consisting of right-angled turns associated with a sharp bend in the body of the parasite (Figure 6A and Video 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Video 11.

claim: No evidence of a ring of inward-directed forces was produced by the TgMyoA knockout parasites.
source: In stark contrast to the wild-type parasites, we also saw no evidence by traction force mapping of a ring of inward-directed forces produced by the TgMyoA knockout parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from traction force mapping of TgMyoA knockout parasites.

claim: No displacement of the matrix above background noise was detected by TgMyoA knockout parasites.
source: In fact, we did not detect any displacement of the matrix above background noise by these parasites (compare Figure 6B to Figure 6D and E; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1, n=16 parasites), suggesting that any forces produced by the moving knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in our traction force assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6D, 6E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 from analysis of 16 parasites.

claim: Any forces produced by the moving TgMyoA knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in the traction force assay.
source: In fact, we did not detect any displacement of the matrix above background noise by these parasites (compare Figure 6B to Figure 6D and E; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1, n=16 parasites), suggesting that any forces produced by the moving knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in our traction force assay.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that no displacement above background was detected.

claim: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA.
source: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 (Gras et al., 2017) is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA, with 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) capable of moving more than one body length (see also Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites and citations to prior work (Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).

claim: 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) are capable of moving more than one body length.
source: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 (Gras et al., 2017) is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA, with 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) capable of moving more than one body length (see also Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites often move in an erratic, stop and start pattern, bending sharply and moving in tightly twisting arcs.
source: However, these parasites often moved in an erratic, stop and start pattern, bending sharply and moving in tightly twisting arcs (Figure 6A and Video 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Video 12.

claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites fail to form constrictions.
source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 from analysis of 36 and 18 parasites respectively.

claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites do not detectably deform the fibrin matrix.
source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 from analysis of 36 and 18 parasites respectively.

claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites can move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites.
source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gras et al., 2017).

claim: Motility is significantly altered, but not completely eliminated, in parasites lacking TgMyoA or TgMIC2.
source: Taken together, these data confirm that motility is significantly altered, but not completely eliminated, in parasites lacking TgMyoA or TgMIC2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced but not absent motility in knockout parasites.

claim: Both TgMyoA and TgMIC2 are required to produce the constrictions and the constriction-associated inward forces on the matrix observed during the motility of wild-type parasites.
source: Furthermore, the data demonstrate that both proteins are required to produce the constrictions and the constriction-associated inward forces on the matrix observed during the motility of wild-type parasites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that knockout of either protein eliminates constrictions and detectable forces.

claim: The nuclei of parasites lacking TgMIC2 do not change shape as they move in 3D.
source: The nuclei of parasites lacking TgMIC2 did not change shape as they moved in 3D (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), providing further evidence that these parasites do not undergo the constrictions seen in wild-type parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Parasites with and without TgMIC2 travel along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively).
source: While parasites with and without TgMIC2 traveled along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively), parasites lacking TgMIC2 moved approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Parasites lacking TgMIC2 move approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites.
source: While parasites with and without TgMIC2 traveled along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively), parasites lacking TgMIC2 moved approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The circumferential zone of attachment to the matrix functions to convert meandering motility into more linear, directed forward progression.
source: These data suggest that the circumferential zone of attachment to the matrix, which requires TgMIC2, functions to convert meandering motility into more linear, directed forward progression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TgMIC2 knockout parasites have less directional movement.

claim: The predominant forces exerted by a moving parasite are periodic and directed in toward the parasite at a fixed circular location within the extracellular matrix.
source: We show here using three-dimensional traction force mapping that the predominant forces exerted by a moving parasite are instead periodic and directed in toward the parasite at a fixed circular location within the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 3D traction force mapping experiments.

claim: The highly localized forces are generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix.
source: These highly localized forces, which are generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix, create a visible constriction in the parasite's plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the direction of the force vectors and the observation of constrictions.

claim: The ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone between the parasite and the matrix, through which the parasite propels itself to move forward.
source: We propose that the ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone between the parasite and the matrix, through which the parasite propels itself to move forward.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In parasites lacking TgMIC2, neither the inward-directed forces nor the constriction of the parasite membrane are observed.
source: In parasites lacking the major surface adhesin, TgMIC2, neither the inward-directed forces nor the constriction of the parasite membrane are observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claim: The trajectories of TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites.
source: The trajectories of the TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites, suggesting that the annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing trajectories of wild-type and TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claim: The annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
source: The trajectories of the TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites, suggesting that the annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TgMIC2 knockout parasites have less directional movement.

claim: Parasites of the phylum Apicomplexa are responsible for approximately one million deaths annually.
source: Parasites of the phylum Apicomplexa cause pervasive human disease and are responsible for approximately one million deaths annually (World Health Organization, 2021; Sow et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (World Health Organization, 2021; Sow et al., 2016).

claim: Toxoplasma gondii is the most prevalent apicomplexan parasite.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is the most prevalent apicomplexan parasite, infecting 30–40% of the human population worldwide (Bigna et al., 2020; Flegr et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bigna et al., 2020; Flegr et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2009).

claim: During invasion of host cells by T. gondii, proteins secreted from the parasite's apical organelles assemble a ring-shaped zone of tight attachment between the membranes of the two cells.
source: During the invasion of host cells by T. gondii and other apicomplexan parasites, proteins secreted from the parasite's apical organelles assemble a ring-shaped zone of tight attachment between the membranes of the two cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about apicomplexan invasion.

claim: The moving junction is anchored to the host cytoskeleton and provides a fixed platform against which the parasite exerts force.
source: This 'moving junction' does not in fact move: it is anchored to the host cytoskeleton and is hypothesized to provide a fixed platform against which the parasite exerts force (Alexander et al., 2005; Besteiro et al., 2011; Dubremetz, 1998; Lebrun et al., 2005; Porchet-Hennere and Torpier, 1983; Aikawa et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alexander et al., 2005; Besteiro et al., 2011; Dubremetz, 1998; Lebrun et al., 2005; Porchet-Hennere and Torpier, 1983; Aikawa et al., 1978).

claim: The body of the parasite narrows dramatically as it passes through the moving junction during invasion.
source: The body of the parasite narrows dramatically as it passes through the moving junction, bearing a striking resemblance to the constrictions we report here during 3D motility.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about parasite invasion.

claim: TgAMA1 and TgRON2 are central players in moving junction formation in T. gondii.
source: Two central players in moving junction formation in T. gondii are TgAMA1, an adhesin secreted onto the parasite surface from the micronemes, and TgRON2, which is secreted by the parasites into the host cell plasma membrane and serves the ligand to which TgAMA1 binds.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about moving junction formation.

claim: Neither TgAMA1 nor TgRON2 plays any detectable role in parasite motility.
source: Neither TgAMA1 (Bargieri et al., 2013; Mital et al., 2005) nor TgRON2 (RVS and GEW, unpublished data) plays any detectable role in parasite motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bargieri et al., 2013; Mital et al., 2005) and unpublished data.

claim: TgMIC2 likely plays an analogous role during motility to that of TgAMA1 during invasion, with TgMIC2 binding to ligands in the extracellular matrix rather than to TgRON2 in the host cell membrane.
source: Instead, TgMIC2 – another microneme protein secreted onto the parasite surface – likely plays an analogous role during motility to that of TgAMA1 during invasion, with TgMIC2 binding to ligands in the extracellular matrix rather than to TgRON2 in the host cell membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with invasion mechanisms.

claim: As the parasite moves forward during both invasion and 3D motility, it simultaneously rotates around its long axis.
source: As the parasite moves forward during both invasion and 3D motility, it simultaneously rotates around its long axis (Leung et al., 2014; Håkansson et al., 1999; Pavlou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Leung et al., 2014; Håkansson et al., 1999; Pavlou et al., 2018).

claim: The TgMyoA motor driving invasion and motility is arranged helically within the parasite, along the spiraling subcortical microtubules.
source: It has long been proposed that the TgMyoA motor driving invasion and motility is arranged helically within the parasite, along the spiraling subcortical microtubules (e.g. Pavlou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Pavlou et al., 2020).

claim: The unique geometry of the parasite periphery can generate a self-organized helical pattern of anterior-to-posterior actin flow.
source: Alternatively, a recent modeling study suggests that the unique geometry of the parasite periphery can generate a self-organized helical pattern of anterior-to-posterior actin flow (Hueschen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hueschen et al., 2022).

claim: If actin filaments flow helically and are connected to the tails of transmembrane adhesins engaged circumferentially with the host cell surface or extracellular matrix, the forward motion of the parasite will be accompanied by rotational twist.
source: In either case, if the actin filaments flow helically and are connected to the tails of transmembrane adhesins engaged circumferentially with the host cell surface or extracellular matrix, the forward motion of the parasite either into the cell or through the matrix will by definition be accompanied by rotational twist.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed mechanism of helical actin flow and circumferential attachment.

claim: Some portion of the perpendicular force directed towards the annular constriction may reflect torque on the matrix produced by the parasite as it twists through this circular zone of attachment.
source: Some portion of the perpendicular force that we observed directed towards the annular constriction in our traction force assays may in fact reflect torque on the matrix produced by the parasite as it twists through this circular zone of attachment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: As a parasite invades a host cell, antibodies are 'shaved' off the parasite surface at the moving junction by an as yet unknown mechanism.
source: As a parasite invades a host cell, antibodies are 'shaved' off the parasite surface at the moving junction by an as yet unknown mechanism (Dubremetz et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dubremetz et al., 1985).

claim: A similar phenomenon of antibody shedding is observed during 3D motility.
source: Remarkably, a similar phenomenon is observed during 3D motility: fluorescent antibody against the surface protein TgSAG1 is lost from the parasite surface anterior to the constriction and shed as a helical trail of fluorescence behind the moving parasite (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10.

claim: 3D motility can be described as the parasite undergoing sequential invasion-like events through circular zones of attachment to the matrix.
source: For example, our data suggest that 3D motility can be best described as the parasite undergoing sequential invasion-like events through circular zones of attachment to the matrix; during invasion the parasite only needs to move a single body length to penetrate into the host cell, but during motility the parasite can string multiple constriction events together to move multiple body lengths (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data suggesting a mechanistic similarity between motility and invasion.

claim: The characteristic constriction of the parasite seen at the moving junction during invasion may reflect the parasite attaching to and pulling on the host cell plasma membrane as it penetrates, rather than being squeezed as it pushes through.
source: The data also raise the possibility that the characteristic constriction of the parasite seen at the moving junction during invasion does not reflect the parasite being squeezed as it pushes itself through the small diameter opening into the host cell, as is commonly thought (e.g. Herm-Götz et al., 2002; Mordue et al., 1999), but rather the parasite attaching to and pulling on the host cell plasma membrane as it penetrates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citations to prior work (Herm-Götz et al., 2002; Mordue et al., 1999).

claim: Actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip of the parasite by formin1.
source: The data presented here with wild-type parasites are at least partially consistent with the linear motor model of motility, in which: (a) actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip of the parasite by formin1 (Tosetti et al., 2019); (b) TgMyoA translocates the actin filaments in an anterior-to- posterior direction along the length of the parasite; and (c) binding of the rearward flowing actin filaments to transmembrane adhesins (Jacot et al., 2016), whose extracellular domains are attached to the substrate, drives the forward motion of the parasite (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claim: Anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery.
source: While anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), we propose a modification to the linear motor model in which force is generated, in whole or in part, by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017).

claim: Force is generated by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
source: While anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), we propose a modification to the linear motor model in which force is generated, in whole or in part, by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
evidence: This is a proposed modification to the linear motor model based on the experimental data.

claim: No anterior-to-posterior bias in the force vectors at the constriction was detected.
source: We were unable to detect any anterior-to-posterior bias in the force vectors at the constriction, which would be expected if the parasite pulls against this zone of attachment in order to move forward.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from traction force mapping.

claim: The regularity with which the parasite generates circular zones of attachment could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip.
source: The regularity with which the parasite generates the circular zones of attachment on its surface, yielding on average one constriction per body length of motion (Figure 5C), could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip (Tosetti et al., 2019) or to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citation to prior work (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claim: The regularity with which the parasite generates circular zones of attachment could be due to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
source: The regularity with which the parasite generates the circular zones of attachment on its surface, yielding on average one constriction per body length of motion (Figure 5C), could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip (Tosetti et al., 2019) or to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: A new constriction may form at the apical tip before the prior constriction has ended, but stalls as the TgMyoA pulls against the adhesive forces of the more posterior previous constriction.
source: Alternatively, the observation that constrictions occur back-to-back almost 50% of the time (Figure 5A), may suggest that a new constriction forms at the apical tip before the prior constriction has ended, but this new constriction stalls as the TgMyoA (or possibly TgMyoH Tosetti et al., 2019) to which it is connected pulls against the adhesive forces of the more posterior previous constriction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citation to prior work (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claim: The lack of a motility-associated constriction in TgMyoA-deficient parasites could reflect an inability to assemble a ring of adhesins at the apical tip or to move through the incipient ring once it has formed.
source: The lack of a motility-associated constriction in TgMyoA-deficient parasites could reflect an inability either to assemble ring of adhesins at the apical tip of these parasites or, more likely, to move through the incipient ring once it has formed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The ring-shaped structures that form during motility may be contractile, and contractility may require TgMyoA.
source: Alternatively, it could be that the ring-shaped structures that form during motility are contractile, and contractility requires TgMyoA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The inward deformation of the fibrin matrix towards the constriction is consistent with a contractile ring.
source: The inward deformation of the fibrin matrix towards the constriction reported here is consistent with a contractile ring, as is the physical constriction of the parasite plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Physical squeezing of the tapering posterior end of the parasite by the narrow constriction may contribute to the parasite's forward motion.
source: This observation suggests that physical squeezing of the tapering posterior end of the parasite by the narrow (and potentially contractile) constriction may contribute to the parasite's forward motion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Both wild-type and mutant parasites may generate small forces distributed over their entire surface that are individually below the level of detection.
source: First, it is possible that both the wild-type and mutant parasites generate small forces distributed over their entire surface (in addition to larger forces that may be generated at the constriction in wildtype), which are collectively sufficient to drive motility but individually below our level of detection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The loss of TgMyoA or TgMIC2 might lead to compensatory changes in the expression of other genes with overlapping or redundant function.
source: Alternatively, the loss of TgMyoA or TgMIC2 might lead to compensatory changes in the expression of other genes with overlapping or redundant function (Meissner et al., 2013; Frénal and Soldati-Favre, 2015; Lamarque et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Meissner et al., 2013; Frénal and Soldati-Favre, 2015; Lamarque et al., 2014).

claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites show changes in the expression of several other microneme and motility-associated proteins.
source: The TgMIC2 KO parasites do in fact show changes in the expression of several other microneme and motility-associated proteins (Gras et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gras et al., 2017).

claim: Parasites lacking TgMyoA and/or TgMIC2 may use a motility mechanism that is entirely different from that of wild-type parasites.
source: Finally, it is possible that parasites lacking TgMyoA and/or TgMIC2 use a motility mechanism that is entirely different from that of wild-type parasites (e.g., Egarter et al., 2014; Gras et al., 2019) and does not involve a constriction but is nevertheless capable of supporting motility and sustaining the parasite's lytic cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Egarter et al., 2014; Gras et al., 2019).

claim: Parasites might use different mechanisms for motility in different situations such as squeezing through tight junctions vs. migrating through loose interstitial tissues.
source: By analogy with observations from animal cells (Lämmermann et al., 2008), parasites might use different mechanisms for motility in different situations such as squeezing through tight junctions (Barragan et al., 2005) vs. migrating through loose interstitial tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Lämmermann et al., 2008; Barragan et al., 2005).

claim: Engagement of T. gondii with the extracellular matrix through a circular band of adhesion may function as part of a guidance system to help the parasite move efficiently through various environments.
source: Engagement of T. gondii with the extracellular matrix through a circular band of adhesion may therefore not only create a fixed platform for the parasite to pull against and move forward; it may also function as part of a guidance system to help the parasite move efficiently through the various environments it encounters as it disseminates through the tissues of the unfortunate organisms it infects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: A curved cell shape and helical trajectory are a particularly efficient way for small cells to move through viscous media.
source: Extensive studies of the helical swimming behavior of bacteria have shown that a curved cell shape and helical trajectory are a particularly efficient way for small cells to move through viscous media (Berg and Turner, 1979; Ferrero and Lee, 1988; Hazell et al., 1986; Kaiser and Doetsch, 1975; Kimsey and Spielman, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Berg and Turner, 1979; Ferrero and Lee, 1988; Hazell et al., 1986; Kaiser and Doetsch, 1975; Kimsey and Spielman, 1990).

claim: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut.
source: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have also previously been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000), suggesting that parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000).

claim: Parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
source: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have also previously been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000), suggesting that parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations in multiple apicomplexan species with citation support (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000).
